### Prerequisites

This text continues the content you have already studied, where we explored the fundamental ideas of comparison. Here we go one step further: we will use those ideas to build classification levels and measure how much two objects resemble each other.

Since each idea builds on the one before it, we recommend reading the previous text first

### Introduction

Look at the animal kingdom — humans included — and one fact becomes obvious: living beings are not all alike. Large differences, such as those between an elephant and a lion, tell us that we are dealing with different species. Small differences, like the ones between the cats in Figure 1, tell us something else: those animals belong to the same species, but to different breeds.
Figure 1: Cirus and Urraca, the editors' cats: the same species, each with its own coat.

Human beings show variations in skin color, eye shape, and many other traits. Yet these differences are not enough to place us in separate species or breeds (<htcite0>; <htcite1>). This raises the central question of this text: how, then, do we build these classifications

Defining a Scale

Figure 2: A centesimal scale: it runs from 0 to 100 in equal steps.

When studying our species and that of chimpanzees, Alan R. Templeton used a branch of mathematics called statistics (<htcite0>; <htcite1>; <htcite2>). So far we have worked only with numbers and the first ideas of limits, so we do not yet have the tools to go deeper into statistics. Even so, we can already grasp some of its basic ideas — and we will need them in the sections ahead

source.text: Staunton, Deborah and Weisstein, Eric W. Statistics

#### Measuring with the Scale

Figure 2, shown here, is similar to Figure 4 of the previous text. However, we will not use it as a conventional ruler for measuring physical dimensions
Figure 3: Metate from Costa Rica — the first object we will measure with our scale. Photograph taken on , during a visit to the Anthropological Museum of San José, Costa Rica.
Now we put the scale to work. We will score 10 characteristics of the object shown in Figure 3, each one worth 10 points, on a scale from 0 to 100:

|Values|Description of the Region |Is it Present?|
|------------|------------|--------------|
|0 - 10| Jaguar shape. | Yes |
|11 - 20| Curved tail pointing downward. | Yes |
|21 - 30| Oval body. | Yes |
|31 - 40| Raised eyes. | Yes |
|41 - 50| Side ornament without a central division. | Yes |
|51 - 60| Elevated ears. | Yes |
|61 - 70| Rounded legs.| Yes |
|71 - 80| Four legs. | Yes |
|81 - 90| Produced between <htdate0> and <htdate1>. | Yes |
|91 - 100| Symmetrical metate. | Yes |
Table 1: The 10 characteristics of the metate in Figure 3 and the value each one receives on the scale.

In this example we listed only a few characteristics and were somewhat flexible with the criteria; in a scientific study the analysis would have to be more rigorous.

Look at the "Is it Present?" column: every characteristic was found, so the scale reaches its maximum value, 100. On a scale like this we often use the word "percent" (symbol "%") to express how much was measured out of the total possible. In other words, this metate shows 100% of the expected characteristics.

#### Near Comparisons

Now we apply exactly the same scale to a second metate, shown in Figure 4:
Figure 4: Metate from El Salvador — a very close match to the one in Figure 3. Photograph taken on , during a visit to the Anthropological Museum of San Salvador, El Salvador.

|Values|Description of the Region |Is it Present?|
|------------|------------|--------------|
|0 - 10| Jaguar shape. | Yes |
|11 - 20| Curved tail pointing downward. | Yes |
|21 - 30| Oval body. | Yes |
|31 - 40| Raised eyes. | Yes |
|41 - 50| Side ornament without a central division. | No |
|51 - 60| Elevated ears. | Yes |
|61 - 70| Rounded legs.| Yes |
|71 - 80| Four legs. | Yes |
|81 - 90| Produced between <htdate0> and <htdate1>. | Yes |
|91 - 100| Symmetrical metate. | Yes |
Table 2: The same 10 characteristics applied to the metate of Figure 4.

This time the characteristic in the range "41-50" was not found. So the metate in Figure 4 matches 9 of the 10 ranges: 9 × 10 = 90 points, that is, 90% of the characteristics defined in the original scale.

#### Distant Comparisons

Now we analyze a metate from a much more distant region: Teotihuacán, Mexico, shown in Figure 5:
Figure 5: Metate from Mexico — the most distant of the three. Photograph taken on , during a visit to the Archaeological Site of Teotihuacán, Mexico.

|Values|Description of the Region |Is it Present?|
|------------|------------|--------------|
|0 - 10| Jaguar shape. | No |
|11 - 20| Curved tail pointing downward. | No |
|21 - 30| Oval body. | No |
|31 - 40| Raised eyes. | No |
|41 - 50| Side ornament without a central division. | No |
|51 - 60| Elevated ears. | No |
|61 - 70| Rounded legs.| No |
|71 - 80| Four legs. | No |
|81 - 90| Produced between <htdate0> and <htdate1>. | No |
|91 - 100| Symmetrical metate. | Yes |
Table 3: The same 10 characteristics applied to the metate of Figure 5.

Here only one characteristic was found, giving a value of 10% on the scale.

#### Interpreting the Results

Let us compare the three results:

- Costa Rica (Figure 3): all 10 characteristics found, so 100%.
- El Salvador (Figure 4): 9 of the 10 found, so 90%.
- Teotihuacán (Figure 5): only 1 of the 10 found, so 10%.

The rule is simple: the closer an object is to the characteristics we defined, the higher its score, moving toward the maximum. The more it deviates from them, the lower its score, moving toward the minimum of 0%. This same rule will let us, in the next section, compare living beings we cannot even see with our eyes.

### Living Beings

#### DNA

To compare species and understand how evolution happened, scientists need one measure that every living thing carries. That measure is DNA: a molecule found in the cells of all living beings, which stores the genetic information of each organism. Because every living thing shares it, DNA has become the foundation of countless scientific studies

source.text: Alberts B, Johnson A, Lewis J, et al.

#### Genetic Differences Among Chimpanzees

Now we can read Alan R. Templeton's research with our scale in mind (<htcite0>). He compared the DNA of different chimpanzee populations and found differences greater than 25%. Remember how the scale works: a gap that large reaches the upper values easily, and it is big enough to distinguish real genetic races within the species.

#### Humans: A Species Without Races

When the same analysis is applied to human DNA, the genetic variation among populations turns out to be less than 5%. On our scale that value stays in the lowest bands: humans are remarkably similar at the genetic level and share more than 95% of their genetic information. Alan R. Templeton goes even further, tracing the genetic history of human populations over time

### Conclusion

In this text we learned how to map information onto a centesimal scale, from 0 to 100, in order to understand how nature works. First we learned to assign characteristics to the scale and to compare objects: each identified characteristic was worth 10 points, so the more characteristics an object had, the closer it came to the maximum, and the fewer it had, the closer it stayed to the minimum.

Then we followed Alan R. Templeton as he tested this idea with genetic samples from chimpanzees and humans. In chimpanzees, genetic differences between individuals could exceed 25%, which is enough to define distinct races. In humans, the same analysis showed differences below 5%: people share at least 95% of their genetic characteristics. That is precisely what invalidates the idea of races within our species.
